exercise1.prompt: A library system: a Book class, and a Library that guards its own collection

cases.name: a book keeps the details it was made with
the program shows the library doing something

hiddenCases.name: Library holds the four operations, and Book holds the details
hiddenCases.describe: a Book class and a Library class with add_book, remove_book, find_book and list_books

hiddenCases.name: a book that was added can be found again
a book that was removed can no longer be found
the collection is not left open to the outside
hiddenCases.call: [a for a in vars(Library()) if not a.startswith("_")]

exercise1.hint: Encapsulation here means the list of books is not something a caller can reach and reorder by hand; every change goes through a method. The name you give the attribute is what says so.

exercise2.prompt: A Shape base class with Rectangle and Circle overriding area(), totalled over a list

cases.name: Rectangle and Circle are both built from Shape and override area
cases.describe: Rectangle(Shape) and Circle(Shape), each with its own area

hiddenCases.name: Shape is the base the two shapes share
hiddenCases.describe: a Shape class with an area of its own

hiddenCases.name: a mixed list of shapes can be totalled without asking what each one is

exercise2.hint: Area is width times height for one shape and pi times radius squared for the other, and the sum does not want to know which is which. If the total is wrong, check each area on its own first.

questions.prompt: The Library stores its books in a private list. Why not just use a public one?
choices: Because every change then has to go through a method, which is where the rules live
Because Python requires it inside classes
To hide the books from other objects entirely
questions.explain: A public list can be appended to from anywhere, so no rule about what a valid book is can be enforced. The methods are the only door.

questions.prompt: sum(shape.area() for shape in shapes) works over a list of rectangles and circles. What makes that possible?
choices: The shapes are all the same class
Every shape has an area method, so the same call is valid for each
sum knows how to measure shapes
Python checks the type of each object first
questions.explain: The loop asks each object for its area and lets the object answer. Adding a Triangle later needs no change to this line.

questions.prompt: Which of these are signs a problem is better modelled with classes than with loose functions?
choices: Several values always travel together and are always passed as a group
The same operations keep being written for things of different kinds
The script is one calculation on two numbers
You want to avoid using functions
questions.explain: Data that travels together wants to be one object, and repeated operations across kinds want a shared base. A single calculation is better off as a function.

questions.prompt: Match each Library method to the question it answers.
questions.explain: Each method names one thing a caller wants to do, which is what keeps the collection itself out of reach.
